key_insight: Large VLMs often give the “right” answer on classic illusions but fail to change that answer when the visual cues are inverted — suggesting many responses come from memorized patterns or spurious correlations rather than true visual perception.
problem_solved: Provides a systematic framework to distinguish whether VLM outputs reflect genuine visual perception or recall of training patterns, resolving ambiguity from prior anecdotal observations of illusion responses.
method: Construct controlled stimuli using classic visual illusions plus engineered inversions that flip the perceptual cue while keeping superficial features similar.
Probe VLMs with standardized prompts across original/inverted pairs and quantify sensitivity using consistency / flip-rate metrics and human baselines.
Complement behavioral tests with attribution analyses (e.g., saliency/attention comparisons) and controls for dataset memorization to attribute failures to perception vs. recall.
impact: Highlights a major limitation of current VLMs — outputs can reflect memorized associations instead of true visual understanding — prompting practitioners to use controlled perceptual tests for robust evaluation and to avoid overtrusting model 'perception' in safety-critical settings.
visual_elements: Side-by-side image pairs (original illusion vs inverted cue) with model answers annotated to show persistence of responses.
Bar chart comparing model flip-rate vs human flip-rate across multiple illusions (sensitivity metric).
Saliency/attention heatmaps overlaid on images to show where models focus in original vs inverted cases.
Simple pipeline diagram: stimulus generation → standardized prompts → behavioral metrics → attribution analyses.
paper_title: Do VLMs Perceive or Recall? Probing Visual Perception vs. Memory with Classic Visual Illusions
paper_authors: Xiaoxiao Sun, Mingyang Li, Kun yuan, Min Woo Sun, Mark Endo
